Intolerant means unwilling or unable to accept something that is different from what you believe, prefer, or are used to.

The easiest way to feel the difference between tolerant and intolerant is this:

A tolerant person says: "I don't agree with you, but I accept that you have the right to think or be that way."

An intolerant person says: "I cannot — or will not — accept that you think or are that way."

Tolerance is the ability to make space for difference. Intolerance is the refusal to make that space.
The three main ways it is used

1. Social and personal attitudes (the most important sense)

This is the most significant and widely used sense of the word. When someone is described as intolerant of a group of people, a religion, a lifestyle, or a set of beliefs, it means they refuse to accept, respect, or peacefully coexist with those people or beliefs. They react with hostility, dismissal, or rejection toward whatever is different from themselves.

Examples:

  • "He is intolerant of people who practice a different religion." — He refuses to accept or respect those who worship differently from him.
  • "The government was intolerant of any political opposition." — It refused to allow dissent to exist at all.
  • "She is deeply intolerant of lifestyles she doesn't understand." — She reacts with hostility to people who live differently from her.

This kind of intolerance sits close to bigotry (a strong, unreasonable dislike of people who are different), narrow-mindedness (refusing to consider other perspectives), and prejudice (judging people negatively without fair reason).

A very important point here: being intolerant is not the same as simply disagreeing. You can disagree with someone's views wholeheartedly and still be tolerant — as long as you accept their right to hold those views. Intolerance goes further. It means you refuse to allow that difference to exist alongside you. It is not just a private feeling; it is an active, rejecting attitude.

2. Everyday behavior and personality

On a less severe level, someone can be intolerant in the sense of having very little patience for something — finding it extremely difficult to put up with, even when it's a small or everyday thing.

Examples:

  • "She is intolerant of rudeness." — Even mild rudeness upsets her deeply; she cannot brush it off.
  • "He is intolerant of noise." — Small sounds bother him greatly; he cannot concentrate or stay calm around them.
  • "My manager is intolerant of delays." — She reacts very strongly to anything that runs late; she has zero patience for it.

In this everyday sense, intolerant is close in meaning to "easily bothered," "impatient," or "having a very low threshold for." It doesn't always carry a moral judgement — it might simply describe someone's temperament or sensitivity toward a particular thing.

3. The medical and biological sense

When a person's body is intolerant of a substance, it means the body cannot properly process or handle that substance — it reacts with symptoms like pain, discomfort, or illness.

Examples:

  • "She is lactose intolerant." — Her body cannot properly digest lactose (the natural sugar found in milk and dairy products), so consuming them makes her unwell.
  • "He is gluten intolerant." — His body reacts badly to gluten (a protein found in wheat and several grains).
  • "She was found to be intolerant to a certain antibiotic." — Her body responds poorly to that medicine.

In this medical sense, the word has nothing to do with attitude or feelings. It is purely about the body's physical inability to process something without a harmful reaction. This is why a doctor might say someone is "intolerant to" a drug or food — they don't mean the person dislikes it, they mean the body rejects it.
The word it pairs with: "of" or "toward"

In all its senses, intolerant almost always comes with the preposition of — and sometimes toward:

  • intolerant of different beliefs
  • intolerant of criticism
  • intolerant toward minority groups
  • intolerant of lactose

This is the natural, correct way to use it in a sentence.

Intolerant is not a black-and-white word — it covers a wide spectrum of intensity.

Someone can be slightly intolerant of something (a little impatient, easily irritated) all the way to deeply or profoundly intolerant (holding strong, active prejudice against a group of people). The same word is used, but the context tells you how serious the intolerance is. Pay attention to words around it: "slightly," "somewhat," "deeply," "fiercely," and "completely" are all common companions that signal how intense the intolerance is.
The direct opposite of intolerant is tolerant — willing to accept, respect, or put up with something that is different from what you believe or prefer, even if you don't like or agree with it.

Intolerance (noun) — the quality or state of being intolerant.
"His intolerance of other cultures made him very difficult to work with."

Intolerantly (adverb) — in an intolerant manner.
"She reacted intolerantly to his suggestion."

Tolerate (verb) — to accept or endure something you may not like.
"He simply could not tolerate the noise."

Intolerable (adjective) — note that this is a different word. It doesn't describe a person's attitude — it describes something that is too bad or painful to be endured. "The heat was intolerable" means the heat was unbearably bad. Do not confuse these two.

Intolerant, in its adjective form, means unwilling or unable to accept something that differs from what one believes, prefers, or is accustomed to. Its most powerful use is social — describing someone who refuses to accept that other people can hold different beliefs, identities, or ways of living. In a softer sense, it describes a person who has very little patience for something that bothers them. And in medicine, it describes a body that cannot handle a particular substance without reacting negatively. In all cases, the word points to a failure to accommodate difference — whether that failure is moral, psychological, or purely physical.
